name: The Frank-Starling Law of the Heart
statement: The more the heart fills, the harder it pumps.
meaning: The stroke volume of the heart increases in response to an increase in the volume of blood filling the ventricles before contraction, when all else is equal. In short, the heart pumps out what it receives: the more blood returns to it and stretches its chambers during filling, the more forcefully it contracts and the more it ejects on the next beat.
mechanism: Greater filling stretches the cardiac muscle fibres, increasing sarcomere length toward an optimum, which increases the force of contraction. The modern account emphasises length-dependent activation: stretch raises the calcium sensitivity of the myofilaments, so more actin-myosin cross-bridges form at a given calcium level, aided by more favourable filament overlap and reduced spacing between the filaments. This is an intrinsic, beat-to-beat property of the muscle itself, requiring no nerves or hormones, that automatically matches output to venous return.

examples.text: The mechanism keeps the left and right ventricles pumping equal volumes over time: if one briefly ejects more, the other receives more, stretches more, and pumps more in turn, self-correcting the balance.
When more blood returns to the heart, greater filling raises end-diastolic volume and stroke volume rises automatically, without any change in nerve or hormone signals.
A premature beat followed by a longer pause allows extra filling, so the next contraction is stronger — a felt demonstration of filling driving force.

variants.name: The length-tension relationship
variants.text: The underlying muscle-physiology principle that a fibre's developed force depends on its length, of which the law is the cardiac expression.

variants.name: The ventricular function curve
variants.text: The plot of stroke volume against filling; there is a family of such curves, shifted up or down by changes in contractility and afterload, not a single fixed one.

whyItMatters: It is a foundational principle of cardiac physiology, explaining how the heart self-regulates output to match the blood returning to it, beat by beat, without external control. It underlies the balancing of the two sides of the circulation and is central to understanding heart failure, in which this compensating mechanism is depressed.

working.text: read stroke volume as rising with the volume filling the ventricle, so more venous return means more output.
understand the balance of the left and right hearts as this mechanism self-correcting any brief mismatch in output.
in heart failure, expect the relationship to be depressed and flattened, so added filling yields little extra output.

limits: There is no single Frank-Starling curve but a family of them: increasing afterload or reducing contractility shifts the relationship down, while inotropic stimulation shifts it up. In heart failure the curve is depressed and flattened, so increased filling produces little or no rise in stroke volume. The mechanism is only the intrinsic component of cardiac regulation; neural and hormonal factors also govern contractility and rate. Beyond an optimal stretch, further filling reduces developed force, though whether the healthy heart normally operates on that descending limb is debated, and the precise molecular basis remains an active research area.
misreadings: It is not the whole story of how the heart is regulated — nerves and hormones also adjust contractility and rate; the law captures only the heart's intrinsic, filling-driven response. And it does not mean more filling is always better: beyond an optimum, overstretch weakens contraction.
origin: Established by Otto Frank, who studied the isolated frog heart in 1895, and Ernest Starling, whose dog heart-lung experiments led to his 1915 Linacre Lecture 'The Law of the Heart,' published in 1918; earlier related observations were made by Bowditch and others.

sources.text: Frank-Starling law, Wikipedia. — the filling-drives-force statement, the length-tension mechanism, and the Frank and Starling origins.
